passages.t: ‘Jesus is Lord’: the test of the Spirit
passages.happening:
Paul takes up another question from their letter. “Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed” (verse 1).

He reminds them of their past. “You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols” (verse 2).

Then he gives a test. “Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be cursed,’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
‘Spiritual gifts’ opens three chapters, 12 to 14. The question seems to have been about the gifts that showed most, above all speaking in tongues. Some in Corinth seem to have counted those who spoke in tongues as more spiritual than others.

Most of the church had once worshipped the gods. A believer from that background might think that any powerful, strange speech must come from God. Paul says no. The idols they once served were ‘mute’. A strong experience proves nothing by itself. What matters is what is said about Jesus.

‘Jesus be cursed’ is a puzzle. The Greek is anathema Iēsous, ‘Jesus is accursed’. Readers have suggested that someone may have shouted it in a frenzy, that it was heard from opponents of the church, or that Paul simply makes up the worst thing anyone could say as a contrast. No one knows for sure.

‘Jesus is Lord’ is one of the earliest Christian confessions. ‘Lord’, kyrios, was a title for the emperor and for the gods, and it was the word the Greek Old Testament used for the LORD, the God of Israel. To say ‘Jesus is Lord’ in Corinth was to give him a loyalty no one else could have. Paul says no one can say it and mean it except by the Spirit.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament mocked idols for their silence. “They have mouths, but cannot speak” (Psalm 115:5). Habakkuk asks what use an idol is, since its maker “makes idols that cannot speak” (Habakkuk 2:18).

‘Jesus is Lord’ gives Jesus the name Israel used for God. Through Isaiah God said, “Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). Paul applies those words to Jesus in another letter: “and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

There is a sad irony in ‘Jesus be cursed’. The Law said, “anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and some used that against a crucified Messiah. Paul answers elsewhere that Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
passages.asks: Paul's test is not how exciting an experience is, but what it says about Jesus. Ask what you are tempted to treat as proof that God is at work. Then ask whether you can say, and mean, ‘Jesus is Lord’ about the whole of your life.

passages.happening:
“There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people” (verses 4-6).

“Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (verse 7).

Paul lists some of the gifts: the message of wisdom, the message of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, the working of miracles, prophecy, distinguishing between spirits, speaking in various tongues, and the interpretation of tongues (verses 8-10).

“All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘Gifts’ is charismata, from charis, grace. A gift of grace is something given freely, not earned. It is not a reward, a badge or proof of being better.

Look at verses 4 to 6. The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God. Paul names the Spirit, the Lord Jesus and God the Father together, as the one source of every gift. Christians later put this into words as the doctrine of the Trinity. Paul does it here without stopping to explain.

‘Manifestation’ means a making visible. A gift is the Spirit showing himself through an ordinary person. And it is ‘for the common good’, for others, not for the one who has it.

Some of the gifts are hard to define today. The ‘message of wisdom’ and the ‘message of knowledge’ may be a word of insight from God for a situation, or teaching that makes God's ways plain; readers differ. ‘Faith’ here is not the faith every believer has, but an unusual trust that God will act. ‘Distinguishing between spirits’ is the gift of telling whether a message comes from God or not.

The Spirit gives ‘as He determines’. No one chooses a gift as a prize. So no one can boast of having one, and no one should despise himself for lacking one.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knows the Spirit giving gifts to particular people for particular work. Of the craftsman who built the tabernacle God said, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). So even skilled hand work can be the Spirit's gift.

Moses longed for more: “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised it would come: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28). Paul writes to a church where that promise has begun to be kept.

And Isaiah foresaw the Messiah on whom the Spirit rests: “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength” (Isaiah 11:2).
passages.hard:
Are these gifts, such as prophecy, healing and tongues, still given today?

Christians who share the same faith in the Holy Spirit answer in different ways. The site's notes on Acts 2 set out the views of Pentecostal, charismatic, continuationist and cessationist Christians in their own terms, and the notes on chapter 13 take up ‘when the perfect comes’ (13:10). These notes do not choose.

All of them agree with what this chapter plainly teaches. The Spirit gives gifts to every believer. The gifts are for the common good. No gift makes anyone better than another. And the confession that Jesus is Lord is the test of true spiritual speech.
passages.asks: Paul says each believer is given something for the good of others. Ask what God has given you that others need: a skill, a kind of care, a way of seeing. And ask whether you use it to serve, or keep it to yourself.

passages.t: ‘In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body’
passages.happening:
“The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ” (verse 12).

“For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Notice the surprise at the end of verse 12. You expect Paul to say ‘so it is with the church’. He says ‘so it is with Christ’. The church is so joined to Christ that it is his body.

Verse 13 names the walls of the ancient world: Jew and Greek, slave and free. In Corinth these divided everyone, from where you sat at dinner to how a court treated you. Paul says all these were baptized into one body and given one Spirit. The walls do not run through the body of Christ.

‘Given one Spirit to drink’ is a picture of water poured out and drunk. It may also recall the pouring of water in baptism. Either way, every believer has received the same Spirit. No one has a larger share.

Paul says ‘we were all’. Every believer, not only some, has been baptized in one Spirit into the one body.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament spoke of the Spirit poured out like water. “For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants” (Isaiah 44:3). Ezekiel promised, “And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).

Israel's own confession, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4), stands behind Paul's stress on ‘one’: one Spirit, one Lord, one God, and so one body.
passages.hard:
What is ‘baptism in the Spirit’, and does verse 13 settle when it happens?

Christians read the phrase in different ways, and these notes do not choose. Many evangelical, Reformed and Baptist Christians hold that verse 13 describes what happens to every believer at the start of the Christian life: by the Spirit each one is joined to the body of Christ. They point to the words ‘we were all’.

Pentecostal Christians, and some charismatic Christians, agree that every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, and also teach that believers may receive a baptism or filling in the Spirit after they come to faith, for power to live and witness. They point to scenes in Acts. Some of them read verse 13 as speaking of the Spirit's work in joining a person to the body, a different thing from the later baptism Jesus gives in the Spirit.

Churches also differ on whether ‘baptized’ here points to water baptism, to the Spirit's inner work, or to both together.

The site's notes on Acts 2 and Acts 8 set out these readings more fully, and the notes on Acts 2:37-41 set out how churches understand baptism.
passages.asks: Paul says Jew and Greek, slave and free, were baptized into one body. Ask who in your church you find it hardest to see as part of the same body as you. And ask what walls of your world you have brought into the church without noticing.

passages.t: Many parts, one body, and honour for the weaker
passages.happening:
“For the body does not consist of one part, but of many” (verse 14). If the foot says, ‘Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body’, it is still part of the body (verse 15). The same is true if the ear says it is not an eye (verse 16).

If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? “But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design” (verse 18).

“The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you.’ Nor can the head say to the feet, ‘I do not need you’” (verse 21). “On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (verse 22). The parts thought less honourable are given greater honour (verse 23). God has given greater honour to the parts that lacked it, “so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another” (verses 24-25).

“If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The body was a well-known picture in the ancient world. The Roman historian Livy told how, when the common people of Rome left the city in protest, a man named Menenius Agrippa persuaded them to return with a fable. The parts of the body, he said, rebelled against the belly, and soon the whole body wasted away. The lesson was that the lower orders should serve the higher. The body was a picture used to keep people in their place.

Paul uses the same picture and turns it over. There are two kinds of people in his body. Some feel they do not belong: the foot that is not a hand. Paul tells them: you belong, whether you feel it or not. Others feel they do not need anyone: the eye that tells the hand ‘I do not need you’. Paul tells them: you are wrong.

Then he goes further. God gives greater honour to the parts that lacked it. In a city that ranked people by wealth, birth and rank, the church was to honour the very ones the city looked down on. The poor who went hungry at the Lord's Supper (11:21-22), the slave, the believer with no impressive gift: these the church must treat with special honour.

‘Mutual concern’ means each part caring for the others. Verse 26 says what that looks like. Pain is shared. Joy is shared. No one suffers alone, and no one's honour is envied.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament already said that God sees the lowly. “Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly” (Psalm 138:6). Hannah sang that God “raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8). Paul's body, where the weaker parts get greater honour, is that same God at work.

Genesis says God formed the human body from the dust and breathed life into it (Genesis 2:7). Paul's ‘God has arranged the members of the body’ (verse 18) echoes the care of the Maker for what he made. “I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14).
passages.asks: Paul writes to two kinds of people: those who feel they do not belong, and those who feel they do not need anyone. Ask which one you are more often. Then ask who in your church is treated as ‘less honourable’, and what you could do this week to give them honour.

passages.t: ‘Now you are the body of Christ’
passages.happening:
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (verse 27).

“And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues” (verse 28).

“Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?” (verses 29-30).

“But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
‘You are the body of Christ’ is said to the church at Corinth, quarrels and all. Paul does not say ‘you should become’ his body. He says ‘you are’.

The list in verse 28 mixes the striking with the ordinary. Apostles and miracles sit beside ‘helping’ and ‘administration’. ‘Administration’ translates kybernēsis, a word related to the Greek for a ship's pilot, the one who steers (the ‘pilot’ of Acts 27:11). Helping and steering are gifts of the Spirit just as much as healing.

Every question in verses 29 and 30 is written in Greek so as to expect the answer ‘no’. Not everyone is an apostle. Not everyone speaks in tongues. No single gift is given to all.

Tongues come last in both of Paul's lists (verses 10 and 28). Many readers think that is on purpose. The Corinthians prized tongues most. Paul puts them at the end, not to despise them, but to put them in their place.

‘The most excellent way’ points to the next chapter. The way above all gifts is love.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament gave Israel many roles: prophets, priests, judges, wise men and women, craftsmen. Each was God's gift to his people. Moses alone could not carry the people, so God shared his Spirit with seventy elders (Numbers 11:16-17, 25).

Paul's other letters give other lists. “We have different gifts according to the grace given us” (Romans 12:6), and there the list includes serving, encouraging, giving and showing mercy. Another says Christ gave “some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11).
passages.hard:
Are these complete lists of the gifts? No. Paul gives different lists in different letters (Romans 12:6-8; Ephesians 4:11; compare 1 Peter 4:10-11), and no two match. Marriage and singleness are each called a gift (charisma) in 7:7. Most readers take the lists as examples, not a full catalogue. Any way the Spirit equips a believer to serve others is a gift.

What about ‘apostles’ today? Most churches hold that the apostles in the first sense, those who had seen the risen Lord and were sent by him (9:1; 15:8), were not replaced. Some churches use the word for missionaries or church planters, and some charismatic churches recognise apostles today. These notes do not choose.

‘Eagerly desire the greater gifts’ is read in two ways. Most take it as a command: seek the gifts that build others up most, like prophecy (14:1). Some read it as a statement: you are eagerly seeking what you think are the greater gifts. Either way Paul moves straight to love.

On whether the gifts continue, see the notes on Acts 2 and on 13:8-12.
passages.asks: Paul asks, ‘Do all speak in tongues?’ and expects no. Ask whether you have measured yourself or others by one gift. And ask what ‘helping’ or ‘steering’ you could offer your church that no one would notice, but that God calls a gift of his Spirit.
